claim: ClpXP is an ATP-dependent protease in which the ClpX AAA+ motor binds, unfolds, and translocates specific protein substrates into the degradation chamber of ClpP.
source: ClpXP is an ATP-dependent protease in which the ClpX AAA+ motor binds, unfolds, and translocates specific protein substrates into the degradation chamber of ClpP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wang et al., 1997; Grimaud et al., 1998; Ortega et al., 2000; Ortega et al., 2002; Sauer and Baker, 2011) and represents established knowledge about ClpXP function.

claim: Subunits in the ClpX hexamer assume a spiral conformation and interact with two-residue segments of substrate in the axial channel.
source: Subunits in the ClpX hexamer assume a spiral conformation and interact with two-residue segments of substrate in the axial channel, as observed for other AAA+ proteases and protein-remodeling machines.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript and by comparison to other AAA+ machines (Puchades et al., 2017; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019; Majumder et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017; Zehr et al., 2017; Han et al., 2017; Monroe et al., 2017; Su et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; White et al., 2018; Cooney et al., 2019; Rizo et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2019; Twomey et al., 2019).

claim: Biochemical and single-molecule biophysical studies indicate that ClpXP operates by a probabilistic mechanism in which five to eight residues are translocated for each ATP hydrolyzed.
source: biochemical and single-molecule biophysical studies indicate that ClpXP operates by a probabilistic mechanism in which five to eight residues are translocated for each ATP hydrolyzed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical and single-molecule studies (Aubin-Tam et al., 2011; Maillard et al., 2011; Sen et al., 2013; Cordova et al., 2014; Olivares et al., 2017).

claim: In the absence of ClpX or another AAA+ partner, small peptides diffuse into the ClpP chamber through narrow axial pores, but larger peptides and native proteins are excluded and escape degradation.
source: In the absence of ClpX or another AAA+ partner, small peptides diffuse into the ClpP chamber through narrow axial pores, but larger peptides and native proteins are excluded and escape degradation (Grimaud et al., 1998; Lee et al., 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work (Grimaud et al., 1998; Lee et al., 2010a).

claim: The substrates of Escherichia coli ClpXP include aberrant ssrA-tagged proteins, produced by abortive translation, and normal cellular proteins synthesized with degradation tags that program rapid turnover.
source: The substrates of Escherichia coli ClpXP include aberrant ssrA-tagged proteins, produced by abortive translation, and normal cellular proteins synthesized with degradation tags that program rapid turnover (Baker and Sauer, 2012; Keiler, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Baker and Sauer, 2012; Keiler, 2015) describing ClpXP substrates.

claim: Single-chain ClpX∆N pseudohexamers support ClpP degradation of ssrA-tagged substrates at rates similar to wild-type ClpX.
source: Single-chain ClpX∆N pseudohexamers, containing six 'subunits' linked by genetically encoded tethers, support ClpP degradation of ssrA-tagged substrates at rates similar to wild-type ClpX (Martin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Martin et al., 2005).

claim: Eliminating ATP hydrolysis in four or five subunits of single-chain pseudohexamers slows but does not prevent ClpP-mediated degradation.
source: Eliminating ATP hydrolysis in four or five subunits of single-chain pseudohexamers slows but does not prevent ClpP-mediated degradation, suggesting that ATP hydrolysis in any one of multiple subunits in the ClpX ring is sufficient to power unfolding and translocation (Martin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Martin et al., 2005).

claim: In optical-trapping experiments using single-chain ClpX and ClpP, the smallest observed translocation steps correspond to movement of five to eight amino acids of the substrate.
source: In optical-trapping experiments using single-chain ClpX and ClpP, the smallest observed translocation steps correspond to movement of five to eight amino acids of the substrate, and kinetic bursts of power strokes produce fast translocation steps two, three, or four-fold larger in terms of the number of residues translocated (Aubin-Tam et al., 2011; Maillard et al., 2011; Sen et al., 2013; Cordova et al., 2014; Olivares et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to optical-trapping experiments (Aubin-Tam et al., 2011; Maillard et al., 2011; Sen et al., 2013; Cordova et al., 2014; Olivares et al., 2017).

claim: Kinetic bursts of power strokes produce fast translocation steps two, three, or four-fold larger in terms of the number of residues translocated.
source: In optical-trapping experiments using single-chain ClpX and ClpP, the smallest observed translocation steps correspond to movement of five to eight amino acids of the substrate, and kinetic bursts of power strokes produce fast translocation steps two, three, or four-fold larger in terms of the number of residues translocated (Aubin-Tam et al., 2011; Maillard et al., 2011; Sen et al., 2013; Cordova et al., 2014; Olivares et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to optical-trapping experiments (Aubin-Tam et al., 2011; Maillard et al., 2011; Sen et al., 2013; Cordova et al., 2014; Olivares et al., 2017).

claim: Kinetic bursts do not occur in repeating patterns, supporting probabilistic but coordinated ATP hydrolysis within the ClpX ring.
source: Such bursts do not occur in repeating patterns, supporting probabilistic but coordinated ATP hydrolysis within the ClpX ring.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that bursts do not occur in repeating patterns, which is cited to prior work (Aubin-Tam et al., 2011; Maillard et al., 2011; Sen et al., 2013; Cordova et al., 2014; Olivares et al., 2017).

claim: The cryo-EM structures show how asymmetric hexameric rings of ClpX dock with symmetric heptameric rings of ClpP.
source: These structures show how asymmetric hexameric rings of ClpX dock with symmetric heptameric rings of ClpP and reveal how the pore-1, pore-2 and RKH loops of ClpX function in substrate binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM structures reveal how the pore-1, pore-2 and RKH loops of ClpX function in substrate binding.
source: These structures show how asymmetric hexameric rings of ClpX dock with symmetric heptameric rings of ClpP and reveal how the pore-1, pore-2 and RKH loops of ClpX function in substrate binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: ClpX adopts a spiral conformation, with neighboring pore-1 loops interacting with every two residues of substrate in the axial channel, as observed in other AAA+ unfolding and remodeling machines.
source: ClpX adopts a spiral conformation, with neighboring pore-1 loops interacting with every two residues of substrate in the axial channel, as observed in other AAA+ unfolding and remodeling machines (Puchades et al., 2017; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019; Majumder et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017; Zehr et al., 2017; Han et al., 2017; Monroe et al., 2017; Su et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; White et al., 2018; Cooney et al., 2019; Rizo et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2019; Twomey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript and by comparison to other AAA+ machines (Puchades et al., 2017; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019; Majumder et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017; Zehr et al., 2017; Han et al., 2017; Monroe et al., 2017; Su et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; White et al., 2018; Cooney et al., 2019; Rizo et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2019; Twomey et al., 2019).

claim: Strictly sequential models of ATP hydrolysis and a power stroke that moves two residues of the substrate per translocation step have been proposed based on structural features of AAA+ unfoldases.
source: Based on these structural features, strictly sequential models of ATP hydrolysis and a power stroke that moves two residues of the substrate per translocation step have been proposed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work proposing such models (Puchades et al., 2017; de la Peña et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2019; Majumder et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017; Zehr et al., 2017; Han et al., 2017; Monroe et al., 2017; Su et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; White et al., 2018; Cooney et al., 2019; Rizo et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2019; Twomey et al., 2019).

claim: An apparent incongruity exists between the structural and functional studies of ClpXP.
source: Thus, an apparent incongruity exists between the structural and functional studies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between structural features suggesting a 2-residue step and functional studies showing 5-8 residue steps.

claim: Experiments using ATP instead of ATPγS resulted in fewer ClpXP complexes.
source: Experiments using ATP instead of ATPγS resulted in fewer ClpXP complexes.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations during sample preparation for cryo-EM.

claim: Substrates were observed in all ClpX∆N structures and probably represent bound endogenous peptides/proteins or partially denatured portions of ClpP or ClpX∆N.
source: Substrates were observed in all ClpX∆N structures and probably represent bound endogenous peptides/proteins or partially denatured portions of ClpP or ClpX∆N.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of substrate density in the cryo-EM structures and speculation about the identity of the substrate.

claim: The six subunits of ClpX∆N formed a shallow spiral (labeled ABCDEF from top to bottom) in all structural classes.
source: The six subunits of ClpX∆N formed a shallow spiral (labeled ABCDEF from top to bottom) in all structural classes, which differed largely in substrate density or nucleotide state, and the hexameric ClpX∆N and heptameric ClpP rings were slightly offset (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 1D.

claim: The hexameric ClpX∆N and heptameric ClpP rings were slightly offset.
source: The six subunits of ClpX∆N formed a shallow spiral (labeled ABCDEF from top to bottom) in all structural classes, which differed largely in substrate density or nucleotide state, and the hexameric ClpX∆N and heptameric ClpP rings were slightly offset (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 1D.

claim: The structure of the ClpX∆N hexamers in the class-1, class-3, and class-4 EM structures were very similar to each other (pair-wise Cα RMSDs 1.2–1.9 Å).
source: The structure of the ClpX∆N hexamers in the class-1, class-3, and class-4 EM structures were very similar to each other (pair-wise Cα RMSDs 1.2–1.9 Å).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The hexamer in the class-2 structure was generally similar (pair-wise Cα RMSDs 2.6 Å) but differed in the position of the 'seam', a dilated inter-subunit interface that occurs as a result of ring closure.
source: The hexamer in the class-2 structure was generally similar (pair-wise Cα RMSDs 2.6 Å) but differed in the position of the 'seam', a dilated inter-subunit interface that occurs as a result of ring closure.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The seam was located between subunits A and B in the class-2 structure and between subunits F and A in the class-1, class-3, and class-4 structures.
source: This seam was located between subunits A and B in the class-2 structure and between subunits F and A in the class-1, class-3, and class-4 structures (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 1E.

claim: The difference in seam position appears to be related to the identity of the nucleotide bound in subunits A or F.
source: As discussed below, this difference appears to be related to the identity of the nucleotide bound in subunits A or F.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural observations and discussed in the context of nucleotide binding.

claim: In both heptameric ClpP rings, the N-terminal residues of each subunit formed a collar of β-hairpins creating a pore into the degradation chamber.
source: In both heptameric ClpP rings, the N-terminal residues of each subunit formed a collar of β-hairpins creating a pore into the degradation chamber (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ClpP had essentially the same structure in the D7 and symmetry-free ClpXP maps.
source: ClpP had essentially the same structure in the D7 and symmetry-free ClpXP maps.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the cryo-EM structures.

claim: ClpX IGF loops are critical for ClpP binding.
source: ClpX IGF loops, named for an Ile268-Gly269-Phe270 sequence, are critical for ClpP binding (Kim et al., 2001; Joshi et al., 2004; Martin et al., 2007; Amor et al., 2019) and were responsible for most contacts in our structures (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kim et al., 2001; Joshi et al., 2004; Martin et al., 2007; Amor et al., 2019) and by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2C.

claim: IGF loops were responsible for most contacts between ClpX and ClpP in the cryo-EM structures.
source: ClpX IGF loops, named for an Ile268-Gly269-Phe270 sequence, are critical for ClpP binding (Kim et al., 2001; Joshi et al., 2004; Martin et al., 2007; Amor et al., 2019) and were responsible for most contacts in our structures (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2C.

claim: IGF loop interactions included packing of the Ile268, Phe270, and Val274 side chains into pockets at interfaces between ClpP subunits.
source: These interactions included packing of the Ile268, Phe270, and Val274 side chains into pockets at interfaces between ClpP subunits (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2D.

claim: I268L, F270L, and V274A variants have severe ClpP binding defects.
source: I268L, F270L, and V274A variants have severe ClpP binding defects (Amor et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Amor et al., 2019).

claim: Asymmetric ClpX-ClpP docking relies on conformational adjustments in the N- and C-terminal residues of individual IGF loops.
source: Asymmetric ClpX-ClpP docking relies on conformational adjustments in the N- and C-terminal residues of individual IGF loops, allowing the central portion of each IGF loop to contact the flat ClpP ring despite projecting from a spiral (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2E.

claim: Changes in IGF-loop length decrease ClpP affinity and degradation activity.
source: Changes in IGF-loop length decrease ClpP affinity and degradation activity (Amor et al., 2019), suggesting that these loops act as shock absorbers to maintain ClpP contacts during ClpXP machine function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Amor et al., 2019).

claim: IGF loops act as shock absorbers to maintain ClpP contacts during ClpXP machine function.
source: Changes in IGF-loop length decrease ClpP affinity and degradation activity (Amor et al., 2019), suggesting that these loops act as shock absorbers to maintain ClpP contacts during ClpXP machine function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that changes in IGF-loop length affect ClpP binding and the structural observation of conformational adjustments in the IGF loops.

claim: In the symmetry-free maps, the unoccupied pocket in each ClpP heptamer was always located between the pockets bound by IGF loops from ClpX subunits E and F.
source: In the symmetry-free maps, the unoccupied pocket in each ClpP heptamer was always located between the pockets bound by IGF loops from ClpX subunits E and F (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Video 1.

claim: The side chain of Arg192 in ClpP appeared to hydrogen bond to the backbone of the IGF loop.
source: In our structures, the side chain of Arg192 in ClpP appeared to hydrogen bond to the backbone of the IGF loop (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2F.

claim: R192KClpP neither bound ClpX∆N in pull-down assays nor degraded protein substrate in the presence of ClpX∆N.
source: Unlike wild-type ClpP, R192KClpP neither bound ClpX∆N in pull-down assays (Figure 2G) nor degraded protein substrate in the presence of ClpX∆N (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2G and Figure 2H.

claim: ADEPs stimulated R192K and wild-type ClpP decapeptide cleavage to similar extents.
source: ADEPs stimulated R192K and wild-type ClpP decapeptide cleavage to similar extents (Figure 2I), establishing that R192KClpP has normal peptidase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2I.

claim: R192KClpP has normal peptidase activity.
source: ADEPs stimulated R192K and wild-type ClpP decapeptide cleavage to similar extents (Figure 2I), establishing that R192KClpP has normal peptidase activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ADEPs stimulate R192K and wild-type ClpP decapeptide cleavage to similar extents.

claim: Arg192 is critical for ClpX binding but not for ADEP binding or ClpP pore opening.
source: Thus, Arg192 is critical for ClpX binding but not for ADEP binding or ClpP pore opening.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that R192KClpP does not bind ClpX but responds normally to ADEP.

claim: Modifying ADEPs to interact with Arg192 may increase affinity for ClpP and improve their efficacy as antibiotics.
source: Modifying ADEPs to interact with Arg192 may increase affinity for ClpP and improve their efficacy as antibiotics.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the structural observation that Arg192 is important for ClpX binding.

claim: ADEP binding to ClpP results both in opening of the axial pore and assembly of its N-terminal sequences into a collar of β-hairpins.
source: Crystal structures show that ADEP binding to ClpP results both in opening of the axial pore and assembly of its N-terminal sequences into a collar of β-hairpins (Li et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior crystal structures (Li et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2010b).

claim: Based on a recent cryo-EM structure of Listeria monocytogenes ClpXP, it was concluded that ClpX binding does not induce the same widening of the ClpP pore as does ADEP binding.
source: Based on a recent cryo-EM structure of Listeria monocytogenes ClpXP, it was concluded that ClpX binding does not induce the same widening of the ClpP pore as does ADEP binding (Gatsogiannis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gatsogiannis et al., 2019).

claim: The ~30 Å diameter and overall structure of the ClpP pore in the E. coli ClpXP structures were extremely similar to the crystal structure of ADEP-activated E. coli ClpP.
source: By contrast, our results support the opposite conclusion, as the ~30 Å diameter and overall structure of the ClpP pore in our E. coli ClpXP structures were extremely similar to the crystal structure of ADEP-activated E. coli ClpP (Li et al., 2010), with an overall RMSDs of 0.8 Å for all Cα's in a single ClpP ring and 0.6 Å for all Cα's of the seven N-terminal β-hairpins and adjacent α-helices that define the pore diameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of the cryo-EM structures to the crystal structure of ADEP-activated ClpP (Li et al., 2010).

claim: All ClpX∆N maps contained substrate density within the axial channel.
source: All ClpX∆N maps contained substrate density within the axial channel, which we generally modeled as an extended poly-alanine chain (Figure 1D), although additional side-chain density of the substrate was modeled as arginine (residue 5) in the class-1 structure and histidine (residue 3) in the class-3 structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 1D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Substrate was built with the N terminus facing ClpP in the class-2 and class-4 structures and in the opposite orientation in the class-1 and class-3 structures.
source: Substrate was built with the N terminus facing ClpP in the class-2 and class-4 structures and in the opposite orientation in the class-1 and class-3 structures.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling of substrate in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: ClpXP can translocate substrates in either the N-to-C or C-to-N direction.
source: ClpXP can translocate substrates in either the N-to-C or C-to-N direction (Olivares et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Olivares et al., 2017).

claim: In all structures, the top of the ClpX channel was most constricted by tight packing between ClpX side chains and substrate.
source: In all structures, the top of the ClpX channel was most constricted by tight packing between ClpX side chains and substrate (Figure 3A–B), providing a structural basis for experiments showing that interactions with substrate near the top of the ClpX channel are most important for unfolding grip (Bell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 3A-B.

claim: Interactions with substrate near the top of the ClpX channel are most important for unfolding grip.
source: In all structures, the top of the ClpX channel was most constricted by tight packing between ClpX side chains and substrate (Figure 3A–B), providing a structural basis for experiments showing that interactions with substrate near the top of the ClpX channel are most important for unfolding grip (Bell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bell et al., 2019) and by the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The class-1 and class-3 structures also had density corresponding to a roughly globular native domain above the channel.
source: The class-1 and class-3 structures also had density corresponding to a roughly globular native domain above the channel (Figure 1C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 1C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The pore-1, pore-2, and RKH loops of ClpX contacted substrate in accord with genetic and biochemical studies.
source: In our structures, the pore-1, pore-2, and RKH loops of ClpX contacted substrate in accord with genetic and biochemical studies (Siddiqui et al., 2004; Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008a; Martin et al., 2008b; Iosefson et al., 2015a; Iosefson et al., 2015b; Rodriguez-Aliaga et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript and by citations to prior genetic and biochemical studies (Siddiqui et al., 2004; Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008a; Martin et al., 2008b; Iosefson et al., 2015a; Iosefson et al., 2015b; Rodriguez-Aliaga et al., 2016).

claim: Substrate was contacted by the pore-1 loops of subunits B/C/D/E in all classes.
source: For example, substrate was contacted by the pore-1 loops of subunits B/C/D/E in all classes, by the pore-1 loop of subunit A in class 4, and by the pore-1 loops of subunit F in classes 1 and 2 (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D, and Video 2.

claim: For each engaged pore-1 loop, the side chains of Tyr153 and Val154 packed between β-carbons spaced two-residues apart on opposite sides of the extended substrate.
source: For each engaged pore-1 loop, the side chains of Tyr153 and Val154 packed between β-carbons spaced two-residues apart on opposite sides of the extended substrate (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D, and Video 2.

claim: From three to five pore-2 loops also contacted substrate, with Val202 making many of these interactions.
source: Depending on the class, from three to five pore-2 loops also contacted substrate, with Val202 making many of these interactions (Figure 4A, B and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 4A, B, D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D, and Video 2.

claim: The RKH loop consisted of an antiparallel β-ribbon stem and a short helix that includes part of the conserved Arg228-Lys229-His230 motif.
source: The RKH loop, which has not been visualized in previous structures and is unique in ClpX-family enzymes (Baker and Sauer, 2012), consisted of an antiparallel β-ribbon stem and a short helix that includes part of the conserved Arg228-Lys229-His230 motif (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 4E.

claim: The RKH loop has not been visualized in previous structures and is unique in ClpX-family enzymes.
source: The RKH loop, which has not been visualized in previous structures and is unique in ClpX-family enzymes (Baker and Sauer, 2012), consisted of an antiparallel β-ribbon stem and a short helix that includes part of the conserved Arg228-Lys229-His230 motif (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Baker and Sauer, 2012) and by the cryo-EM structures.

claim: When contacting the globular portion of substrate above the pore, the RKH loops mimicked adjustable structural jacks supporting a house during foundation repair.
source: When contacting the globular portion of substrate above the pore, the RKH loops mimicked adjustable structural jacks supporting a house during foundation repair (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is a metaphorical description based on the structural observation of RKH loops contacting substrate above the pore.

claim: The RKH loops alter substrate specificity.
source: The RKH loops alter substrate specificity (Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008a), but whether they are critical determinants of substrate binding is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Farrell et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008a).

claim: The most severe RKH-loop mutant (RKH→AAA) did not support ClpP degradation of an ssrA-tagged substrate and hydrolyzed ATP ~5 fold faster than the parent.
source: The most severe mutant (RKH→AAA) did not support ClpP degradation of an ssrA-tagged substrate and hydrolyzed ATP ~5 fold faster than the parent (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 4F-G.

claim: Changing RKH to AKH, KHR, or KRH slowed degradation.
source: Changing RKH to AKH, KHR, or KRH slowed degradation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 4F.

claim: A variant [RKH2-AAA]2 pseudohexamer with four wild-type RKH loops and two AAA mutations had a ~3 fold higher KM for substrate degradation than the parent and hydrolyzed ATP slightly faster.
source: A variant [RKH2-AAA]2 pseudohexamer with four wild-type RKH loops and two AAA mutations had a ~3 fold higher KM for substrate degradation than the parent and hydrolyzed ATP slightly faster (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 4G-H.

claim: The RKH loops play important roles in substrate recognition and in regulating rates of ATP hydrolysis.
source: Thus, the RKH loops play important roles in substrate recognition and in regulating rates of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that RKH-loop mutations affect substrate degradation and ATP hydrolysis rates.

claim: Density for ATPγS was observed in five subunits of each ClpX∆N hexamer.
source: We observed density for ATPγS in five subunits of each ClpX∆N hexamer (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1-Table S2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1-Table S2.

claim: In the sixth subunit, bound nucleotide density fit best as ADP, which is a 10–15% contaminant in ATPγS preparations.
source: In the sixth subunit, bound nucleotide density fit best as ADP, which is a 10–15% contaminant in ATPγS preparations, but was slightly less convincing than ATPγS density in other subunits (Figure 5B; Supplementary file 1-Table S2), raising the possibility of averaging of multiple nucleotide-binding states.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 5B and Supplementary file 1-Table S2, and by knowledge about ATPγS preparations.

claim: 'ADP-bound' subunits had poorly structured channel loops, made fewer contacts with substrate and with neighboring subunits, and were offset from the axis of the hexamer by ~2.5 Å.
source: 'ADP-bound' subunits had poorly structured channel loops, made fewer contacts with substrate and with neighboring subunits, and were offset from the axis of the hexamer by ~2.5 Å (Figure 5C–E; Supplementary file 1-Table S3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 5C-E and Supplementary file 1-Table S3.

claim: Side-chain contacts with nucleotide included ClpX residues Val78-Ile79 (box-II), Lys125-Thr126-Leu127 (Walker A), Asp184-Gln185 (Walker B with E185Q mutation), Arg307 (arginine finger), and Arg370 (sensor-II).
source: Side-chain contacts with nucleotide included ClpX residues Val78-Ile79 (box-II), Lys125-Thr126-Leu127 (Walker A), Asp184-Gln185 (Walker B with E185Q mutation), Arg307 (arginine finger), and Arg370 (sensor-II) (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 5A, B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: V78A/I79A, E185Q, and R370K mutations eliminate ATP hydrolysis or weaken nucleotide binding.
source: V78A/I79A, E185Q, and R370K mutations eliminate ATP hydrolysis or weaken nucleotide binding (Joshi et al., 2004; Hersch et al., 2005; Martin et al., 2005; Stinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Joshi et al., 2004; Hersch et al., 2005; Martin et al., 2005; Stinson et al., 2013).

source: We found that K125M, T126A, L127A, D184A, and R307A mutations also severely inhibited ATP hydrolysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
